background.definition: Acute gastroenteritis is a clinical syndrome characterized by the rapid onset of diarrhea, with or without vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain.

list.listitem: In US children, acute gastroenteritis accounts for more than 1.5 million outpatient visits, 200,000 hospitalizations, and 300 deaths per year.
Rotavirus diarrhea accounts for $250 million per year in direct health care costs, with $1 billion in total costs to society.
Viral (70%-80%): rotavirus (most common cause in children younger than 5 years), adenovirus, Norwalk virus, calicivirus, astrovirus, parvovirus.
Bacterial (10%-20%): Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter jejuni, Yersinia enterocolitica, Escherichia coli, Clostridioides difficile.
Parasitic (up to 10%): Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium.
Viruses damage the villous brush border of the small intestine, causing impaired carbohydrate digestion and malabsorption with excessive loss of fluid from the intestine (osmotic diarrhea).
Some viruses also produce secretory and/or promotility toxins.
Viral gastroenteritis is spread by the fecal-oral route.
Routine immunization for rotavirus is recommended with either a 2 or 3 dose series of orally administered vaccine at 2 and 4 months or 2, 4, and 6 months respectively. A
Vaccination is likewise recommended for premature infants who are at least 6 weeks old, medically stable, and ready to be discharged from the hospital. B

Patients and parents should be educated about good hand washing as an important preventative measure against disease transmission, and should keep oral rehydration solutions at home for use at the onset of symptoms. C
Clinical history and physical examination should be the basis for diagnosing acute gastroenteritis and degree of dehydration. Laboratory tests are not routinely recommended. C
Combinations of findings are most effective in diagnosing dehydration. See . B
Testing for etiologic agents is not routinely recommended, but stool studies should be considered in certain circumstances. See . C

Consider other diagnoses and further treatment in patients who appear toxic, have diarrhea for more than 7 days, are immunocompromised, have chronic disease including metabolic disorders, are failing to thrive, or have hyponatremic or hypernatremic dehydration. C

list.listitem: The clinical history should assess onset, frequency, and character (bloody, watery, bilious) of diarrhea and emesis; oral intake; urine output; presence of fever; mental status; and weight before illness. Past medical history may identify complicating factors.

The physical examination should include vital signs, weight, appearance of eyes and mucous membranes, respiratory pattern (deep respirations suggest metabolic acidosis), and an abdominal examination including assessment of bowel sounds for ileus, capillary refill, and skin turgor.
Signs that rule in dehydration (of greater than or equal to 5%) are prolonged capillary refill, prolonged skin tenting/turgor, abnormal respiratory pattern, absent tears, and cool extremities.
Parental report of normal urine output is strong evidence against significant dehydration (LR− = .04).
Laboratory tests are generally not helpful in diagnosing or treating gastroenteritis. Stool assays to determine etiologic agent rarely change management.

Serum chemistry values are useful only if markedly abnormal (ie, BUN >45 mg/dL), although a normal serum bicarbonate makes dehydration very unlikely. The routine use of serum chemistry values is not recommended in the evaluation of the child with acute gastroenteritis.

Consider a stool culture and an ova and parasite examination in patients with grossly bloody stools, high fever, diarrhea has not improved by day 7, the child is immunocompromised, you suspect septicemia, there is a history of foreign travel, or during known community outbreaks. Consider a C. difficile toxin assay in patient with recent antibiotic exposure.
Combinations of findings are most effective in diagnosing dehydration. See .

A validated clinical decision rule found that patients having at least 2 of the following 4 signs are likely to be at least 5% dehydrated (LR+ = 6.1): prolonged capillary refill, dry mucous membranes, absent tears, and abnormal general appearance.
Degree of dehydration is the most important diagnosis to make when viral gastroenteritis is suspected.
shows a recommended approach for diagnosing and treating dehydration from acute gastroenteritis.
Oral rehydration is the mainstay of therapy.
Ondansetron safely reduces vomiting in children, increases the ability to receive oral fluids, and reduces the risk of hospitalizaiton.
Oral rehydration solutions should be first-line therapy for all dehydrated patients, except those with severe dehydration or obtunded mental status who require IV hydration. A
Ondansetron (oral or IV) reduces emesis, facilitates rehydration, and reduces the need for IV rehydration and hospitalization.B
Other antiemetics and antidiarrheals are not recommended for use in children. C

Antidiarrheals are not recommended in the routine management of gastroenteritis. Efficacy data are limited in children, and side effects such as ileus, drowsiness, and nausea may interfere with oral rehydration.

Ondansetron is a cost-effective way to reduce vomiting in children with gastroenteritis. A systematic review of 10 randomized trials with 1215 participants found that it increased the likelihood of cessation of vomiting at 1 hour (RR 1.5, 95% CI 1.2-1.9), reduced the likelihood of failure of oral rehydration (RR 0.5, 95% CI 0.4 - 0.7), the need for IV rehydration (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.31-0.63), and reduced the risk of hospitalization (RR 0.5, 95% CI 0.3-0.97). Dosage is similar with IV or oral administration: 0.15 mg per kg, which is usually rounded to 2, 4, or 8 mg when given orally. Consider using oral disintegrating tablets if available, even in young children.

Routine antibiotic use should be avoided since antibiotics are associated with hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) when used to treat E. coli 0157:H7 diarrhea. However, acute watery diarrhea confirmed or presumed to be of bacterial etiology may benefit from azithromycin treatment.
The American Gastroenterological Association guidelines for use of probiotics (2020) recommend against their use for acute infectious gastroenteritis.

A large, well-designed trial not sponsored by industry randomized 971 children 3 months to 4 years with acute gastroenteritis to Lactobillus rhamnosus GG or placebo and found no difference regarding the likelihood of moderate or severe symptoms, duration, or frequency of diarrhea.

A second study in the same issue of the journal compared a combination of Lactobacillus rhamnosus R0011 and L. helveticus R0052, at a dose of 4.0×109 colony-forming units twice daily with placebo in children with moderate to severe acute gastroenteritis, and found no benefit for the probiotic.

Cochrane reviews have found conflicting evidence on whether probiotics shorten the duration of acute diarrhea. One found that that probiotics shorten the duration of acute diarrhea by 30 hours and decrease the risk of diarrhea by the third day of illness. Another found that probiotics probably make little or no difference for patients with diarrhea lasting 48 hours or longer. However, many of these studies were small, unblinded, and/or industry funded.
Oral rehydration solutions (ORS) should be first-line therapy for all dehydrated patients, except those with obtunded mental status or those unable to keep up with ongoing losses.

A meta-analysis shows that when comparing oral versus IV rehydration, there are no significant differences in duration of diarrhea, total fluid intake, or electrolyte abnormalities. Failure rate for oral rehydration solutions was 4%. For every 25 children (95% CI, 14-100) treated with ORT, one would fail and require IV rehydration.

The target ORS volume is 50 to 100 mL/kg body weight over 2 to 4 hours, plus replacement of ongoing losses (10 mL/kg per episode of diarrhea or emesis). Begin with small frequent volumes of 5 to 10 mL every few minutes and increase as tolerated.

Appropriate ORS contains at least 45 mEq/L of sodium, as well as adequate potassium and carbohydrate, with osmolarity ≤270. Examples are Pedialyte, Rehydralyte, or WHO-ORS packets. Inappropriate solutions include Gatorade and other sports drinks, soda, juices, or broths.

Patients with gastroenteritis should be offered their usual age-appropriate diet as soon as rehydration is complete (within 4-6 hours). A large multicenter study showed no difference in frequency of vomiting or diarrhea between patients with immediate versus late (24 hours) refeeding. Restrictive diets such as clear liquids, the BRAT diet, lactose-free foods, or diluted feedings are not recommended.
Regular diet may be supplemented with oral rehydration solutions while emesis or diarrhea continues, with a goal of 10 mL/kg per emesis or stool.

In low-resource countries with high rates of zinc deficiency, zinc supplementation for 7 days during a diarrheal episode decreases diarrhea incidence and diarrhea hospitalization, and decreases mortality by 23%.

In high-resource countries, an RCT in children with no dehydration and mild gastroenteritis found that dilute apple juice followed by their preferred fluids was associated with fewer treatment failures within 7 days of treatment (16.7% vs 25%; difference: –8.3%; 97.5% CI: –∞ to –2%), including decreased need for IVF rehydration (2.5% vs 9%; difference: –6.5%; 99% CI: –11.6% to –18%) than electrolyte maintenance solutions.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that polymer-based ORS (eg, prepared using rice or wheat) compared to glucose-based ORS (with osmolarity ≤270) may decrease diarrhea volume in the first 24 h by 24 ml/kg and may decrease diarrhea duration by 8 hours, but had no difference in risk of unscheduled IVF.
Consider hospital admission in the following situations: inadequate home care, oral intake less than ongoing losses, complicating illness, or severe dehydration (>10%).
Also consider hospitalization if no reliable follow-up is available or if you feel the need for close observation (eg, young infants, mental status changes, diagnostic uncertainty).
Offer usual diet after 4 hours to 6 hours of therapy or as soon as patient is rehydrated.

Continue IV fluids plus oral rehydration solutions to meet maintenance needs, as well as ongoing losses through stool or emesis. If the patient is not hypernatremic at presentation, use an isotonic solution (NS or D5NS) for IVF replacement and maintenance. As a reminder, maintenance needs are calculated as (100-50-20 mL/kg/d): 100 mL/kg/d for 1st 10 kg + 50 mL/kg/d for 2nd 10 kg + 20 mL/kg/d for any remaining kg. (For example, an 8 kg infant's maintenance needs would be 100 mL/kg/d x 8 kg = 800 mL/d = 33 mL/h. An 18 kg child's maintenance needs would be (100 mL/kg/d x 10 kg) + (50 mL/kg/d x 8 kg) = 1000 mL + 400 mL = 1400 mL/d = 58 mL/h. A 28 kg infant's maintenance needs would be (100 mL/kg/d x 10 kg) + (50 mL/kg/d x 10 kg) + (20 mL/kg/d x 8 kg) = 1000 mL + 500 mL + 160 mL = 1660 mL/d = 69 mL/h.) Estimates should be similar when using the (4-2-1 mL/kg/h) maintenance needs formula: 4 mL/kg/h for 1st 10 kg + 2 mL/kg/h for 2nd 10 kg + 1 mL/kg/h for remaining kg. (For example, an 8 kg infant's maintenance needs would be 4 mL/kg/h x 8 kg = 32 mL/h; 18 kg child's maintenance needs would be (4 mL/kg/h x 10 kg) + (2 mL/kg/h x 8) = 40 mL + 16 mL = 56 mL/h; 28 kg child's maintenance needs would be (4 mL/kg/h x 10 kg) + (2 mL/kg/h x 10 kg) + (1 mL/kg/h x 8 mg) = 40 mL + 20 mL + 8 mL = 68 mL/h).
Consider giving the ORS solution via a nasogastric tube if the patient is unable to drink it or if they vomit persistently.
Consider discharge when patient is rehydrated, has adequate oral intake to balance ongoing losses, and has available follow-up.
Viral gastroenteritis is a self-limited disease that usually resolves within 3 to 10 days. C
Since there is no treatment for viral gastroenteritis other than managing symptoms, prognosis and natural history are the same. C
Children with acute gastroenteritis (AGE) are more likely to develop disorders of gut-brain interactions (formally called functional GI disorders) compared with controls.

Parents should be educated about the signs of dehydration for which to seek further care. Patients can return to school or daycare when fever and vomiting are absent for 24 hours and stools can be adequately contained. C

cell.label: Determine degree of dehydration: How many of the following signs are present? Dry mucous membranes, absent tears, prolonged capillary refill, ill appearance.
Feed usual diet. If vomiting, offer small frequent amounts multiple times per hour.
Risk of bacterial infection? - Bloody stools? - High fever? - Foreign travel? - Community outbreak? - Recent antibiotics?

Consider stool culture, ova and parasites, C. dificile toxin. Use antibiotics* if a causative organism is isolated. *Do not use antibiotics for E. coli 0157:H7 diarrhea, as this has been associated with hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS).
Parent and patient education: - Return to school or daycare - Prevention of infection.
Give ORS 50 to 100 mL/kg over 3 to 4 hours, plus 10 mL/kg per stool or emesis. Begin with 5 to 10 mL every 5 minutes and increase as tolerated.
Consider ondansetron (0.15 mg/kg) PO or IV, if vomiting.
Oral intake sufficient for ongoing losses?

Give 20 mL/kg NS or LR in repeated boluses until perfusion and/or mental status improve, then D5 NS to replace fluid until able to take PO. (With urine output, consider adding KCl to IVF until able to take PO - D5NS + 10-20 MEq KCl/L). Consider checking basic metabolic panel. Correct hypo/hypernatremia if present.
Resume regular diet once rehydrated. Consider continuing ORS 10 mL/kg per stool or emesis.
Treat with IV fluids or NG ORS.
Consider checking basic metabolic panel. Correct hypo/hypernatremia if present.
